Loss Functions · In the News06

Programming Day 01: Architecture

Our model has a single layer, going from a <1, 784> input vector down to a <1, 10> output vector. The equation for a single layer is the bottom row: z = X @ ωT + b.

Loss Functions · Review07

McCulloch–Pitts Artificial Neuron (1943)

What a neural network is trying to model is the way a human brain works, by combining and chaining together artificial neurons in layers.

  • Layer: a group of neurons that process inputs in parallel and pass their outputs to another layer.
  • Neuron: a computational unit with a set of parameters (weights and biases) that creates a weighted sum of the input.
Loss Functions · Review08

A McCulloch–Pitts Neuron

The weighted sum inside the cell body is the same linear transformation as our layer, one neuron at a time.

Loss Functions · Review09

Artificial Neurons

Our model could be said to have 1 layer with 10 neurons, with each neuron producing one of the output numbers.

Loss Functions · Review10

Producing an Output Prediction

We have 10 possible outputs (targets/classes) that we can produce, one for each number.

Loss Functions · Outputs11

Representing an Output Prediction and the Ground Truth

We return the largest index value as our prediction (3 in this case), which we refer to as ŷ.

Our ground truth vector is a one-hot vector with the same size as the output vector, with a 1 in the correct index and 0s everywhere else. We refer to this vector as y.

Loss Functions · Outputs12

Softmax and Logits

On Friday we saw an additional function called Softmax, whose purpose was to transform our <1, 10> output vector into a probability distribution. Before we apply the softmax function, our output is called logits.

  • Logits: the model's raw, unnormalized outputs, with one dimension for each possible class.
  • Softmax: a function that converts logits into nonnegative probabilities that sum to 1.
Loss Functions · Outputs13

Loss Functions

  • Loss: a single numerical measure of how well a model's prediction matches the expected answer.
  • Loss Function: a function that calculates our Loss. Cross-Entropy is the loss function we'll use primarily in this course.
\mathcal{L}_{ce} = -\sum_{i=1}^{10} y_i \cdot \log(\yhat_i)

Cross-Entropy: the loss function used to train LLMs is called "Cross-Entropy Loss" and it's one of the most common loss functions. Heavily based on the principle of "entropy" as used in Information Theory, it's a measure of how surprising our answer is relative to our ground truth, based on the entropy formula −∑ p(x) log2 p(x). Mostly outside the scope of the class, but it's really not that complicated.

Loss Functions · Loss16

Mathematical Formulation of a Neural Network

We can write our loss as a function of our input and parameters:

2.356 = \mathcal{L}_{ce} = -\sum_{i=1}^{10} y_i \cdot \log(\text{softmax}(X \Omega\T + b)_i)

Formulating a neural network mathematically in this manner is critical to actually training one. Wednesday we'll dig more into this, and it will be the "mathiest" lecture in this course.

Loss Functions · Loss17

Training a Neural Network

Over the course of many epochs (one training "step" of a neural network), we'd expect to see our loss steadily decrease, which is indicative of our predictions getting better.

Loss Functions · Training18

Training a Model

Training a model lets it practice over and over on the same set of data, ideally improving its performance over time! It does this by updating its parameters.
